title: Int8/AWQ/FP8 regression hypothesis & playbook — KV cache + batching on-prem
summary: Deep-dive to triage post-quantization accuracy regressions observed after migrating a 13B model to INT8/AWQ hybrid on their on-prem VPC. Discussed hypotheses around KV cache staleness, batching-induced prefix misalignment, attention kernel numerical differences for FP8 paths, and differences between GPTQ and AWQ per-layer behavior. Agreed on prioritized experiments (layerwise delta, cold vs warm KV runs, deterministic micro-batches) and a short playbook for rollback and canarying. Next steps: Diego to run layer diffs, Maria to collect failing prompt set, Redwood to share kernel micro-benchmarks and a canary config template.
topics: INT8 vs AWQ vs FP8 tradeoffs
next_steps: Diego to run layerwise output-diff and share CSV by 2027-03-06
Maria to upload canonical failing prompt set to shared drive by 2027-03-04
Redwood (Evan) to send micro-benchmark kernels and FP8 numerical notes by 2027-03-05
Schedule follow-up triage on 2027-03-08 at 9am PT
action_items: Diego Morales: run layerwise output diffs for top-100 failing prompts (due 2027-03-06)
Maria Chen: collect and label 1000 failing prompts + expected vs actual examples (due 2027-03-04)
Evan Park: export runtime kernel timings and FP8/INT8 variance notes (due 2027-03-05)
Rina Kapoor / Samir Gupta: produce infra repro script (docker + kernel flags) and baseline logs (due 2027-03-07)
Samantha Ortiz: compile playbook draft and share with stakeholders (due 2027-03-09)
transcript:
[00:00] Samantha Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we sent the agenda — quick intro?
[00:12] Maria Chen: Hi all, Maria here. We've been seeing a silent accuracy drop after converting our 13B baseline to INT8 with AWQ hybrid, noticed in production last week.
[00:25] Diego Morales: Got it. Can you describe the symptoms — is it hallucination increase, token-level mismatch, or throughput mismatch?
[00:36] Leah Patel: Mostly output divergence — the model used to return a structured list and now sometimes mixes up items, small but unacceptable regressions for our scoring pipeline. Latency seems fine.
[00:49] Omar Haddad: To be clear, this is on-prem VPC, using Redwood Private with dedicated infra — we did a model swap and kept the same routing.
[01:02] Samantha Ortiz: Thanks. Quick run of attendees — Diego (SE), Evan (product), Rina (SRE) from our side. On customer side Maria, Omar, Leah, Samir and Nadia.
[01:16] Diego Morales: Okay, high level — there are a few common root causes when you see silent drops post-quant: quantization algorithm mismatches (GPTQ vs AWQ layer effects), runtime kernel numerical differences (FP8 path vs INT8 path), KV cache interactions with batching, and also prompt/caching alignment issues when micro-batching prefixes.
[01:37] Maria Chen: We mainly used AWQ for MLP layers and int8 for attention, it's a hybrid we got from bench notes. We also enabled prefix caching to speed long-doc runs.
[01:50] Diego Morales: That combo can expose tricky failure modes — especially if KV cache warms with different precision or if sequence alignment shifts across micro-batches.
[02:03] [00:02] (laughter, crosstalk)
[02:15] Leah Patel: Can you explain what you mean by alignment shift? We didn't change prompts.
[02:22] Diego Morales: Sure — imagine batching two requests with different prefix lengths; if the runtime's KV cache coalescing or caching key indices gets mis-indexed by a small off-by-one between INT8 kernels and FP32 baseline, later tokens effectively attend to wrong cached keys. It often manifests as subtle token swaps.
[02:46] Maria Chen: Hmm ok. We do burst-batch to maximize throughput during nightly jobs — could be that.
[02:55] Evan Park: One other vector is per-layer dequantization rounding differences — AWQ sometimes uses stochastic rounding for activations and that produces slightly different distributions relative to GPTQ which uses symmetric quant mapping. If your regression is distribution-sensitive it can show up.
[03:17] Omar Haddad: Our infra logs show KV cache hit ratio is high, but we also had recent host kernel updates (CUDA + custom kernel flags) — could runtime changes be a factor?
[03:29] Rina Kapoor: We pushed 2 kernel updates last week to optimize MM kernels — worth flagging.
[03:35] Diego Morales: Yes, runtime kernel changes absolutely can change numerics, especially if fused attention kernels use FP8 fast-paths with reduced accumulation precision. We should capture kernel versions and exact build flags.
[03:50] Nadia: Also we observed regressions more frequently on longer context (>1k tokens).
[03:57] Diego Morales: That aligns with KV cache interacting with quantization because longer contexts rely heavily on prefix caching.
[04:05] Samantha Ortiz: Let's sketch hypotheses — Diego?
[04:10] Diego Morales: Hypothesis A: KV cache staleness / mis-indexing due to batching/coalescing differences between precision paths. Hypothesis B: Layerwise quantization sensitivity — certain layers (usually early attention layers or mid-MLP) amplify small numeric differences. Hypothesis C: Runtime kernel numeric divergence in FP8 fast-paths causing accumulation rounding that cascades. Hypothesis D: Prompt set exposes brittle outputs — loss surface near a bifurcation where tiny numeric diffs flip token choice.
[04:44] Maria Chen: Good list. We want to know priority experiments to isolate.
[04:49] Diego Morales: Priority 1: Deterministic single-request cold runs vs hot runs. Run each prompt single-threaded with KV cold (no cache) and warm (pre-warmed). Compare token-level deltas. Priority 2: Layerwise output diffs — run FP32 baseline and quantized model, dump activations per layer and compute L2/diff and argmax changes. Priority 3: Micro-batch decomposition — reproduce the micro-batching pattern from infra and run with deterministic scheduling to see misalignment. Priority 4: Kernel/version lock — run on a known-good kernel build and compare to current.
[05:25] Omar Haddad: For priority 2, how heavy is activation dump? We have infra limits.
[05:31] Diego Morales: For 13B it's okay for a sample of 100 prompts, and we can limit to top-k layers (we suspect layers 6-10 and 22-26, but we'll probe). We'll produce scripts that stream diffs rather than full dumps.
[05:48] Maria Chen: We can start with 100 prompts. We'll flag the top 20 failing ones.
[05:54] Samantha Ortiz: Good. Evan, can Redwood produce the layer-diff helper?
[05:58] Evan Park: Yes, Diego has a helper script we can adapt; I'll attach it to the drive and include kernel profiling notes. We'll also share an example canary config for on-prem to run incremental rollouts per-precision.
[06:13] [06:13] (typing)
[06:20] Leah Patel: A practical question — if we find a few bad layers, what's the recommended mitigation? Rollback quant for those layers?
[06:28] Diego Morales: Options: fallback to FP32/FP16 for suspect layers, selective per-layer dequantization, or use a mixed-precision scheduling where you run those layers on a higher-precision kernel. There's also latency tradeoffs.
[06:40] Rina Kapoor: We can't afford a huge latency hit — we have an SLO of p95 < 180ms for inference.
[06:47] Diego Morales: Understood — we can do per-route canarying: route 5-10% traffic to the higher-precision variant and measure regression rate. Also apply caching gating: disable KV cache for routes with high regression sensitivity.
[06:59] Omar Haddad: Disabling KV cache would blow cost but it's for triage.
[07:04] Samantha Ortiz: Right, triage only. We'll outline the playbook.
[07:09] Diego Morales: Another detail — AWQ's per-channel scale uses asymmetric params; if your dequant in runtime uses a different rounding scheme from the quant offline, mismatch occurs. Confirm the quantization metadata (scale/zero points) persisted with the model and that your runtime reads them in the same endianness/format.
[07:31] Maria Chen: We persisted the .awq artifacts from conversion. Omar, can you confirm they were uploaded intact?
[07:36] Omar Haddad: I checked SHA sums, they matched the artifact storage.
[07:42] Diego Morales: Good. Still, kernel-level dequant/unpack code path differences matter. We'll capture the exact bytes read by the runtime if needed.
[07:52] Nadia: We saw more flakiness on GPU nodes with mixed CPU+GPU memory pressure. Could memory pressure cause KV cache eviction anomalies?
[08:02] Samir Gupta: We do have a GC setting that evicts older mmapped pages under high memory pressure.
[08:09] Diego Morales: That could create partial KV warm states. If eviction occurs mid-request, and runtime continues with a stale pointer but partial updates, you'll get corrupted keys. We'll look for spikes in mem pressure correlated with regression events.
[08:24] Samantha Ortiz: Ok — prioritize logs correlation then.
[08:28] Diego Morales: For the layerwise bisect I'd do this workflow: run baseline FP32 -> save per-layer logits for the prefix and first 64 tokens of generation; run quantized -> compute per-layer L2 and top-1 argmax flips; rank layers by severity; then test fallback of top-3 layers to FP32/FP16 in runtime to see if outputs recover.
[08:53] Maria Chen: Sounds good. How many prompts do we need for statistical confidence?
[08:58] Diego Morales: Start with 100 failing prompts, and a control set of 300 random prompts — that'll give a decent signal. For p-values we'd need more but initial triage is fine with 100/300.
[09:12] Evan Park: We'll provide the scripts to compute both per-token divergence and a simple semantic diff metric (n-gram overlap + embedding cosine for expected vs actual) — to catch small surface changes that are semantically relevant.
[09:27] Leah Patel: Embedding cosine is helpful — some numeric diffs don't matter.
[09:31] Diego Morales: Exactly. Also be wary of temperature and sampling differences — ensure determinism by using greedy/top-k=1 if you want consistent comparisons.
[09:42] Maria Chen: Our production uses top-p and temperature 0.4 for creative tasks — should we force deterministic?
[09:50] Diego Morales: For diffs, yes. For measuring user-impact, keep production sampling and measure downstream metric delta.
[09:58] Samantha Ortiz: Let's talk about reproducibility — we need a docker+kernel flag repro. Rina/Samir?
[10:05] Rina Kapoor: We'll capture the container hash and kernel module versions. Samir will script the repro with env flags.
[10:12] Samir Gupta: Yep. We'll also log nvprof/ruff timings as requested.
[10:17] Diego Morales: Another diagnostic: run with KV cache disabled completely and compare failure rate. If disabling resolves it almost entirely, KV interaction is likely root. If not, it's per-layer quant sensitivity.
[10:31] Maria Chen: We did a partial test where we disabled cache on a small sample and saw fewer hallucinations, but it wasn't conclusive.
[10:39] Diego Morales: Good hint. Take that as initial evidence pointing to hypothesis A.
[10:45] Evan Park: If hypothesis A holds, mitigation options: adjust coalescing window, tighten index guards, or mark certain routes as cache-protected (i.e., only allow caching when prefix length stable). That reduces throughput but is surgical.
[11:02] Omar Haddad: Coalescing window? We currently coalesce 10ms of incoming requests per worker to batch.
[11:09] Diego Morales: That coalescing window is likely the culprit — near-simultaneous requests with slightly different prefix alignments can cause the runtime to mis-assign cache offsets if there isn't robust indexing. We can disable coalescing for sensitive routes or reduce window.
[11:24] Maria Chen: Reduce to 1ms?
[11:27] Diego Morales: Start with turning off for one route. If that reduces error, you can then experiment with 2ms and so forth.
[11:34] Nadia: We also have per-node network jitter that may reorder request arrival times.
[11:40] Diego Morales: That complicates coalescing assumptions. We'll capture arrival timestamps at the worker boundary.
[11:46] Samantha Ortiz: Any other kernel-level traps?
[11:49] Diego Morales: Watch out for fused attention kernels that assume aligned memory layouts; quantized weight packing requires strict alignment — different compiler flags can change struct padding and cause subtle misreads, especially if you mix released runtime builds compiled with different flags. Ensure the runtime and kernel were built from the same git tag.
[12:10] Evan Park: We'll share our kernel-build manifest.
[12:14] Diego Morales: Great. Also AWQ sometimes stores scales per-output channel which, if accidentally interpreted transposed vs non-transposed at load time, will produce channel-swapped dequantization. That is a binary failure mode but can appear subtle if only a few channels are swapped.
[12:33] Maria Chen: That would be a big issue — we didn't see obvious wholesale swap.
[12:36] Diego Morales: Right, but partial transposition bugs in weight packing sometimes only affect subset of layers due to caching of packed blocks. We'll check.
[12:45] Samantha Ortiz: Let's capture the exact artifact read hashes in runtime logs to be safe.
[12:51] Rina Kapoor: We'll add that to the repro script.
[12:54] [12:54] (typing)
[13:07] Leah Patel: Walk me through the canary rollback playbook briefly.
[13:12] Diego Morales: Canary playbook: 1) Canary conversion — create a precision-variant model variant with metadata flag and deploy to canary pool. 2) Route 5% traffic with mirrored logging. 3) Collect per-request diffs and runtime metrics. 4) If regression > threshold (we recommend >0.5% top-1 flip for structured outputs) then rollback the canary variant and mark suspect layers. 5) For temporary mitigation you can enable per-layer fallback or disable KV cache for the route.
[13:46] Maria Chen: What's a reasonable metric threshold? 0.5% you said?
[13:50] Diego Morales: For structured outputs maybe 0.2-0.5% matters depending on business impact — you set risk tolerance. For free-text maybe 1%.
[13:59] Samir Gupta: We'll start with 0.4% for our scoring pipeline.
[14:03] Diego Morales: Also add downstream metric checks — e.g., re-scoring mismatch rate.
[14:08] Evan Park: We'll create a canary template you can drop into your route config that isolates precision variants and toggles KV caching flags per route.
[14:18] Maria Chen: Awesome. On the experimental side, what's the expected runtime overhead for per-layer FP fallback?
[14:25] Diego Morales: Depends on layer count. Fallback of top-1 layer might add 3-8% latency, top-3 maybe 12-25% — that's very workload dependent. We'll quantify on your infra.
[14:39] Omar Haddad: We need to be able to measure that precisely to decide tradeoffs.
[14:43] Diego Morales: We'll include microbenchmarks for top-1/top-3 fallback cases.
[14:49] Nadia: Any notes on AWQ vs GPTQ — do tradeoffs point one way?
[14:54] Diego Morales: AWQ often gives practical better MSE and works well on activations, but AWQ's asymmetric scales can be more sensitive to dequant code path differences. GPTQ yields different per-layer error profiles; sometimes converting to GPTQ and re-running bisect can alleviate layer flips. But that requires retrain-like conversion and check. So try AWQ diagnostic first then possibly GPTQ re-conversion if suspect layers persist.
[15:20] Maria Chen: We used AWQ because bench improved latency.
[15:24] Diego Morales: Understandable. For rollback produce a GPTQ variant of just suspect layers? It's possible to selectively re-quantize layers, but tooling varies.
[15:33] Samantha Ortiz: Let's make the experiment plan explicit in the playbook.
[15:37] Diego Morales: Plan: 1) Repro repro: produce docker+kernel script (Samir/Rina). 2) Deterministic cold vs warm KV runs (Maria + Diego). 3) Layerwise diffs (Diego). 4) Canary with per-route coalescing disabled (Redwood + Infra). 5) Microbench fallback measurements for top-1/top-3 fallback (Redwood). 6) If needed, try GPTQ partial re-quant for top layers.
[16:03] Maria Chen: Timeline? We want a mitigation within 2 weeks ideally.
[16:08] Samantha Ortiz: Timeline seems feasible: initial diffs + repro in 1 week, canary second week.
[16:14] Evan Park: We'll staff Diego and Evan for analysis and Diego will drive the scripts. I'll attach kernel manifests and the canary config template after the call.
[16:24] Leah Patel: Any quick wins we can try right now?
[16:27] Diego Morales: Immediate quick win: disable coalescing for one high-risk route and toggle KV caching off for a small sample during peak runs — that should reveal whether caching/coalescing is central. Another quick check: run a few deterministic runs with greedily decoding.
[16:43] Maria Chen: We'll do the coalescing toggle now. Omar will do it.
[16:46] Omar Haddad: I'll schedule the toggle and report back in 24 hours.
[16:51] Samantha Ortiz: Great. Diego — can you share the layer-diff helper after?
[16:55] Diego Morales: Yes, I'll upload to the shared drive with README and example outputs.
[17:01] Samantha Ortiz: Any other questions?
[17:04] Maria Chen: One small item — we saw one node with older gcc toolchain that wasn't updated; could that introduce packing mismatch?
[17:11] Diego Morales: It could if the packing used different struct alignment. We'll ask Samir to ensure homogenous toolchain across canary pool.
[17:19] Samir Gupta: Will check.
[17:22] Evan Park: I'll also provide a binary checksum validator to gate firmware/toolchain drift.
[17:29] Nadia: Should we capture more telemetry like per-layer activation histograms in prod?
[17:36] Diego Morales: Good idea but heavy — for prod maybe sample 0.1% of requests to capture histograms. For canary capture 100%.
[17:45] Samantha Ortiz: Ok we've got a lot. Quick recap of next steps?
[17:49] Maria Chen: (over speaking) yes please —
[17:51] Samantha Ortiz: Diego to run layerwise diffs & share by Mar 6; Maria to upload failing prompts by Mar 4; Evan to share kernel manifests and canary template by Mar 5; Rina/Samir to produce repro script and ensure toolchain homogeneity by Mar 7; Samantha to draft playbook by Mar 9; schedule follow-up on Mar 8 9am PT.
[18:13] Maria Chen: Thank you, appreciated.
[18:16] Omar Haddad: Thanks all.
[18:18] Leah Patel: Thanks.
[18:20] Diego Morales: Thanks, we'll be in touch.
[18:22] [End of recording]
